stimulus.title: Hướng dẫn tham quan Hartley House
stimulus.audio_script:
Guide: Good morning and welcome to Hartley House. Before we begin, let me tell you a little about the place. The house was built in 1782 for a wealthy merchant called Thomas Hartley. Many visitors assume he lived here with a large family, but in fact he never married, and he mainly used the house to entertain business partners. After his death, it became a school for girls, and it stayed a school until 1950, when the town council bought it.
Guide: Today the house is run by volunteers. We have around sixty of them, and most are retired teachers, which seems fitting given the building's history.
Guide: Now, a few practical points. The tour of the house takes about forty-five minutes. Photography is fine everywhere except in the library, because the old books can be damaged by the flash. If you need a break, the café is in the old kitchen on the ground floor, and it serves lunch until half past two.
Guide: Let me now explain the gardens. When you leave the house by the back door, you'll see the rose garden directly in front of you. To the left of the rose garden is the lake, and on the far side of the lake you'll find the boathouse, which now holds an exhibition of old photographs of the house. The children's play area is to the right of the rose garden, next to the greenhouse, where our gardeners grow plants that you can buy. And finally, if you follow the path past the greenhouse, you'll come to the gift shop, near the car park.

stimulus.audio_script:
Presenter: And now some news about the Greenford Summer Festival, which takes place on the first weekend of July in Victoria Park. This year's theme is "Around the World", so you can expect music, dance and food from more than twenty countries.
Presenter: Things get started on Saturday morning with a parade at ten o'clock. It leaves from the railway station and finishes at the park gates about an hour later. Inside the park, the food market will have around forty stalls this year.
Presenter: Entry to the park is free, but if you'd like to watch the concerts on the main stage, you'll need a wristband, which costs five pounds. Children under ten don't need one.
Presenter: Parking near the park is very limited, so the council is running a park-and-ride service from Hillside Retail Park. Buses will leave every twenty minutes from eight in the morning.
Presenter: The organisers are still looking for about thirty more volunteers, especially for litter picking. If you can help, you can sign up at the town hall or on the festival website.
Presenter: If you're coming with young children, there will be a lost children point near the main gate. And finally, if there's heavy rain, events will move indoors to the sports hall at Greenford Academy, so the festival will go ahead whatever the weather.

Emma: Jack, have you had a chance to look at the survey results?
Jack: Yes. I was surprised that so few people cycle to campus. Only twelve percent.
Emma: Me too, given how many bike racks there are. Though I suppose the hill on the way here puts people off.

Emma: Right. For the presentation, I think we should start with a short video of the morning queue at the bus stop, rather than with a chart.

Emma: Let's do those together. They're the most important part.

stimulus.title: Sinh viên trao đổi với giảng viên hướng dẫn
stimulus.audio_script:
Dr Lewis: Come in, Sophie. So, how's the research project going?
Sophie: Quite well, I think. I've finished the literature review, but it's much longer than it should be.
Dr Lewis: Then you'll need to cut it. Focus on studies from the last ten years. Some of the older ones are no longer relevant.
Sophie: OK. For my own study, I'm planning to use a questionnaire about phone use and sleep.
Dr Lewis: That's fine, but people tend to underestimate how long they spend on their phones. Could you also ask participants to share the screen-time data from their phones?
Sophie: That's a good idea. I'll add that.
Dr Lewis: How many participants are you aiming for?
Sophie: I was hoping for a hundred, but so far only forty have agreed.
Dr Lewis: Try the first-year students. They're usually keen to help. You could put a notice in the student newsletter.
Sophie: I'll do that. Another thing: I'm not sure how to present the results.
Dr Lewis: For this kind of data, a scatter graph would work best. Avoid pie charts.
Sophie: And should I include interviews as well?
Dr Lewis: Only if you have time. A few short interviews could add depth, but the questionnaire should be your main source.
Sophie: Right. And the final deadline is still the end of April?
Dr Lewis: Yes, the thirtieth. But please send me a draft of your methods chapter by the end of March.

stimulus.title: Bài giảng: đảo nhiệt đô thị. Viết MỘT TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT SỐ cho mỗi câu.
stimulus.audio_script:
Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about urban heat islands, which is the reason cities are often warmer than the countryside around them. On a summer evening, the centre of a large city can be as much as seven degrees Celsius warmer than nearby rural areas.
Lecturer: There are several causes. The first is the materials we build with. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. The second is the lack of vegetation. Trees and plants cool the air through a process called evapotranspiration, in which water evaporates from their leaves. Thirdly, heat is produced directly by human activity, by cars, air conditioners and factories.
Lecturer: Why does this matter? Higher temperatures increase energy use, as people turn on air conditioning, and they also affect health. Older people are particularly at risk during heatwaves. Hot weather can also make air quality worse, because it speeds up the formation of ground-level ozone.
Lecturer: So what can cities do? One solution is the cool roof, a roof painted white or covered with a reflective material. In one study in Los Angeles, cool roofs reduced indoor temperatures by up to three degrees. Another solution is the green roof, which is covered with plants. Green roofs also help to reduce flooding by absorbing rainwater. Planting trees along streets is perhaps the simplest approach: the shade from trees can lower the temperature of pavements by more than ten degrees.

stimulus.title: Bài giảng: container vận tải. Viết MỘT TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT SỐ cho mỗi câu.
stimulus.audio_script:
Lecturer: In this lecture, I'll look at an invention that changed world trade: the shipping container. Before the 1950s, goods were loaded onto ships piece by piece, as sacks, barrels and boxes carried by teams of workers called dockers. Loading a single ship could take a week, and theft was common.
Lecturer: The modern container was developed by an American businessman, Malcolm McLean, who owned a trucking company. In 1956, his first container ship sailed from New Jersey to Texas carrying fifty-eight containers. The key idea was simple: the same steel box could move from a truck to a ship to a train without being opened.
Lecturer: The impact was enormous. The cost of loading cargo fell by more than ninety percent. Ports had to change completely. They needed huge cranes and large areas of flat land to store containers, so many old ports in city centres closed, and new ones were built outside cities. This also meant that thousands of dockers lost their jobs.
Lecturer: Standardisation was the next important step. In the late 1960s, international organisations agreed on standard sizes. The most common unit today is the twenty-foot equivalent unit, or TEU, and the largest modern ships can carry more than twenty-four thousand of them.
Lecturer: Containers have also had environmental effects. Shipping is relatively efficient for each tonne of cargo, but the industry still produces around three percent of global carbon emissions. Researchers are now testing ships powered by ammonia, and even by sails.
